paras: The threatened lynching of John Taylor took place at Chattanooga, Tennessee, on the evening of April 6, 1881, when a large crowd met Taylor, a prisoner accused of murder, on his arrival by train amid talk of lynching him. Officers lodged him in jail without harm. The crowd drew one sentence at the end of a Knoxville report on his capture, which the papers treated as the news.

In mid-February 1881 Taylor, a steamboat man from Roane County, was accused of killing Capt. John Fletcher, an old steamboat man, at Chattanooga and escaping. The Knoxville Daily Chronicle wrote that he had killed Fletcher "about a trivial matter" and called him "a desperate and dangerous man." Chattanooga residents raised a reward subscription, and Governor Hawkins offered $250 for his arrest.

Acting on information received on Tuesday, April 5, Hamilton County Sheriff H. J. Springfield took a posse of six by train to Loudon, where Loudon County Sheriff Joe D. Foute and three others joined them. At daylight they found Taylor asleep at the home of a Mr. Van Stowe on the Clinch River, and after first seeming ready to fight he surrendered. A dispatch from Charleston that day reported the Chattanooga jailer passing on the train with the prisoner.

News of the capture caused "great excitement" in Chattanooga, according to the Chronicle. When Taylor arrived on the 6:30 train that Wednesday evening, there was "an immense jam and confusion, and intimaions [intimations] of lynching, but the prisoner was safely jailed." No account names anyone in the crowd or describes any attempt to take him.

After several trials and mistrials, Taylor was sentenced at Chattanooga to ten years in the penitentiary for manslaughter and appealed. On September 14, 1882, while being taken to the Supreme Court at Knoxville, he was freed from the train by his brothers, who killed Sheriff W. T. Cate and Deputy John J. Conway.

The crowd appears in only one paper, the Knoxville Daily Chronicle of April 8, 1881, which ran Taylor's capture under the headlines "The Capture of Taylor, the Murderer" and "Capture of a Murderer." The Chronicle praised Sheriff Springfield as "one of the most efficient officials in the State" and passed over the lynching talk without comment. The Cleveland Weekly Herald gave the arrest a single line a week later and did not mention a crowd. No paper stated the race of Taylor or of Fletcher.

Early news briefs in the Wheeling Register and the Mower County Transcript reversed the February killing, reporting that Taylor had been "shot dead" by Fletcher. The Knoxville paper, closer to the scene, and the later trial reports name Taylor as the killer. Accounts also differ on where he was taken, with the Chronicle's dispatch placing it in Roane County and the Cleveland paper in Loudon County.

framing.detail: Headlines 'The Capture of Taylor, the Murderer' and 'Capture of a Murderer' treated the guilt as settled and the arrest as the story; the lynching talk got one sentence and no comment.
